analysis.one_liner: Lets pharmacists and wholesalers import cheaper prescription drugs from other countries.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and its Health Subcommittee and never received a hearing, markup, or vote before the 107th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would rewrite federal drug law so that American pharmacists and drug wholesalers could legally import prescription drugs from other countries, where the same medicines often sell for far less. It removes a requirement that the Secretary of Health and Human Services first prove to Congress that such imports are safe and would save consumers money, and it directs the Secretary to write the rules to run the import program within a year of enactment. It also adds labeling rules so imported packages must show the country of origin and the names and addresses of the importer and exporter.
analysis.who_benefits: Americans who fill prescriptions, especially seniors and people on fixed incomes paying U.S. retail prices that are often several times higher than prices for the identical drugs in Canada and Europe. Licensed pharmacists and wholesalers gain a new legal line of business bringing in lower-priced medicines.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Americans paying high U.S. drug prices

how_it_helps.text: Strikes the part of federal law that blocked drug importation unless the Secretary of Health and Human Services demonstrated to Congress that imported products are safe and that allowing them would financially benefit consumers, which was the main legal barrier to a working import program.

Requires the Secretary to issue a final rule carrying out the import program within one year of enactment, with an effective date no later than 30 days after the rule is issued, so the program could not be left unimplemented.
Adds labeling rules requiring imported drugs to identify the country of origin, the importer, and the exporter, giving regulators and consumers a way to trace where the product came from.

analysis.who_pays: Brand-name drug manufacturers, which charge much higher prices in the United States than abroad; a functioning import channel would let Americans buy the same drugs at foreign prices, cutting into that price gap. Wholesalers and pharmacies would bear the cost of compliance with the new labeling rules.

drawbacks.text: Safety is the core objection: the bill deletes the requirement that the Secretary demonstrate to Congress that imported products are safe and would actually save consumers money before the program starts, leaving opponents without that up-front check.

Some imported drugs come through secondary distributors and could be counterfeit, expired, or mishandled; the bill's labeling rules identify who handled the package but do not itself guarantee testing or inspection of every product.

Drug companies could respond by limiting the supply they sell to Canadian and other foreign pharmacies, a commonly reported response to importation pressure, which could shrink the supply available to import and leave foreign patients shorter on medicine.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For consumers, the benefit is straightforward: the same FDA-approved medicines sold at far lower foreign prices. The cost side is real but limited to safety risk from a supply chain that is harder to oversee, a risk the bill tries to manage with origin and handler labeling rather than eliminating. On the evidence in the record, the consumer benefit is large and the manageable safety cost is comparatively small.

outcome.mechanism: It sat in committee: the House referred it to Energy and Commerce, which sent it to its Health Subcommittee, and it died there when the 107th Congress ended in early January 2003.

narrative.text: Rep. Marion Berry (D-AR) introduced the bill on October 2, 2002, with 13 cosponsors, including 11 Democrats and 2 Republicans.
The same day, the House referred it to the Committee on Energy and Commerce.
On October 28, 2002, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Health, where no further action is recorded.
The 107th Congress ended on January 3, 2003, and the bill never received a markup, a committee vote, or a floor vote.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Brand-name drug makers, who kept their much higher U.S. prices in place because the bill never advanced. American consumers who might have bought lower-priced imported drugs stayed where they were.

for.name: Rep. Marion Berry
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to implement the drug importation program under section 804 of the Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act.

for.name: 13 House cosponsors
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; 11 of 208 House Democrats and 2 of 223 House Republicans signed on.

against.name: Billy Tauzin
against.role: Chair, House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.what_they_did: His committee received the bill on the day it was introduced and never reported it out or scheduled a markup before Congress ended; a former pharmaceutical industry staffer and, later, industry lobbyist, he chaired the panel with jurisdiction over the bill.

against.name: Brand-name pharmaceutical industry
against.what_they_did: Opposed drug importation measures during this period, arguing they posed safety risks and would undercut U.S. drug prices.

sides.party_line_note: Sponsorship crossed party lines but was thin: 11 of 208 House Democrats and 2 of 223 House Republicans cosponsored, and no vote was ever taken to test broader support.

industries.note: These companies charge far higher prices in the United States than for the same drugs sold abroad; legal importation would expose the U.S. price gap and cut into that revenue. Their interest in blocking it runs directly against consumers paying U.S. prices.
The bill authorizes pharmacists and wholesalers to import covered products, creating a new legal line of business; they would also bear modest labeling-compliance costs.
A functioning import program would route new U.S. demand to foreign pharmacies, though manufacturers limiting supply to them could strain availability for local patients.
